articles.summary: Some people spent the week leading up to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI replaying the old games. I, sicko that I am, spent it watching TV news coverage of the franchise from the past 20 years. Grand Theft Auto has been a staple of cable and broadcast TV news since at least the release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001. I’ve been an adult for all of it; I’ve had a front row seat for two decades of moral panics, parental freakouts, and bizarre political theater. The games and the broader culture’s reaction to them have changed dramatically in that time. In 2001, newscasters worried GTA III was training an army of young men to kill. In 2026, The New York Times earnestly quoted Bell Hooks in its review of GTA VI. For mainstream news, GTA is the ur-video game. The open world that mirrors our own, the prevalence of sex and death, and the increasingly realistic simulations and graphics pointed towards the dream of what a video game could be. articles.author: Reed Albergotti
articles.summary: Reed’s view Anthropic’s IPO went on as well as anyone could have reasonably hoped. It was up 17% over its initial price with a valuation of about $1.3 trillion, making it the biggest debut in history. But Anthropic shares are down 11% so far today, and the rest of the market is down, too, as skepticism of the AI trade builds. The funny thing is, there are a lot of people in the tech industry who say they would actually like to see things slow down. That’s because all of the resources are being funneled into a small group of companies building essentially the same product, leaving little room for other ideas. The “tokenmaxxing” craze earlier this year has accelerated revenue growth at the frontier labs and hyperscalers. But if every unit of computer memory and every accelerator is concentrated among only a handful of players, innovation — and AI adoption — starts to slow down.
